reviews.review_rationale: Re-derived: every legal deletion removes an even number of -1s so the parity of m=#(-1) is invariant; the terminal positions are the empty array and a lone -1, and an independent memoised solver I wrote (n<=12, all 8190 arrays) confirms the P-positions are exactly empty and 1^k(-1)1^k, so the O(n) case split (m even: delete everything; m odd: keep q1 or qm and trim so the survivor is centred; m==1 with a==b is the loss) is correct and the emitted (L,R) always leaves a P-position. All four samples reproduce (two with a different but verified winning move; the problem is special-judged). All three labels are the technique: a real two-player choice, a parity invariant that decides the game, and the explicit winning move is the actual work.

drop.label: greedy
drop.why: proposer confidence 0.6 and the 'greedy' is just one of many ways to distribute a deficit over a contiguous range of achievable sums; there is no exchange argument and a searcher for greedy would learn nothing here

reviews.review_rationale: Re-derived the bound: before the i-th accepted rank r_i there are r_i-1 edges, i-1 of them merges, so the r_i-i internal edges must fit inside components built by i-1 merges (max C(i,2)-(i-1) free pairs), giving i<=r_i<=C(i,2)+1; growing one blob realises every increasing vector obeying it, and the caps grow so the sums are contiguous in [N(N-1)/2, N-1+N(N-1)(N-2)/6]. Checked the emitted matrices with my own Prim for every N<=8 and every K<=N^3, and 200k random permutations at N=5 hit exactly {10..14}. Samples (2,1),(2,8),(3,2),(3,3),(3,4) all reproduce. Kruskal's acceptance structure is genuinely the key idea, so kruskal stays alongside minimum-spanning-tree and constructive-algorithm.

drop.label: combinatorics
drop.why: the count is 2^B once the forced vertices are identified; the work is the structural characterisation on the virtual forest and the online maintenance, not a combinatorial argument. A combinatorics searcher landing on an online virtual-tree data-structure problem would be misled

reviews.review_rationale: Re-derived the characterisation: with T LCA-closed, f(S)=T iff S contains every vertex of T with <=1 virtual child (leaves cannot be generated; a one-child vertex is never the LCA of two elements of f(S) subset T; a vertex with >=2 virtual children has forced leaves in two distinct child subtrees so it is free), hence 2^B; and T is closed iff every tin-adjacent pair's LCA lies in T, with cnt[u]=number of virtual children for u in T because the T-elements of u's subtree follow u contiguously in DFS order. Independent subset-enumeration brute force with parent-walk LCA agreed on 1949 toggles over 300 random trees, both samples reproduce, O((N+Q) log N) is comfortable. virtual-tree, lca, the DFS-order adjacent-pair trick (euler-tour) and the predecessor/successor set (ordered-set) are each load-bearing.

drop.label: constructive-algorithm
drop.why: nothing is constructed or output; the achievability half is an existence argument inside a min+count problem, and a searcher for constructive problems wants to build an object

drop.label: modular-arithmetic
drop.why: the modulus only wraps factorials and binomials for output; scaffolding, not the technique

drop.label: parity-argument
drop.why: confidence 0.6; that a cycle crosses a cut an even number of times is a tautology, and the H lower bound comes from the top bit, not from parity

drop.label: graph-modeling
drop.why: confidence 0.55, below the gate; reading a cyclic permutation as a Hamiltonian cycle is the statement, not a modelling insight

reviews.review_rationale: Re-derived the H = top power of two lower bound (any cycle must cross the high/low cut and every crossing carries that bit), the K = M-1 free pairs {j, H+j}, the M==1 and M==2 exceptions (answer H+2), and the matching-pairs-glued-into-one-cycle count times path-system placements. My own permutation brute force for N=2..9 (all N! permutations) matches solve() exactly, the proposer's independent bitmask DP matches for N<=14, and all seven samples reproduce including N=17. The technique is the top-bit cut argument plus the cycle-counting combinatorics; the rest of the proposed labels are scaffolding.

drop.label: tin-tout-ancestor-check
drop.why: confidence 0.5, below the gate, and the proposer concedes the solution needs a dynamic reachability test rather than a static tin/tout compare

reviews.review_rationale: The reduction (each kid picks either edge j_i->i or the pair i->l_i, l_i->j_i plus i->j_i; safe iff some choice is acyclic; output any topological order) is correct, and the branching search over the A-edges of a found cycle is complete and sound, so verdicts and orders are right (the proposer's exhaustive n<=5 and my re-reading agree). But the complexity argument does not hold: the write-up rests on 'the search never exceeded 9 nodes' from random instances where impossibility is rare, and I constructed a family (chain 1..m with j_1=m, a side leaf s_i under each chain node, l_v=s_{v-1}, l_{s_i}=i+1, l_{s_m}=1) that is impossible and drives the verified script to exactly n+1 search nodes, each an O(n) pass: 0.54s at n=1600 and quadratic growth, i.e. hours at n=200000. The proposal must either give the cycle-local implementation with an amortisation argument that total work is near-linear, or switch to the published linear approach, before this can publish.
issues: complexity claim falsified: the verified search is Theta(n) nodes x O(n) per node on an explicit impossible family (skeptic scratchpad kg2_family.py); '9 search nodes' is an artefact of random testing

the 'fresh cycle iff j_v reaches l_v down the tree' criterion is only valid at the first flip level; deeper levels create cycles through B-edges (e.g. flipped v with l_v equal to a flipped child), so a linear implementation needs more structure than the write-up describes

drop.label: graph-modeling
drop.why: confidence 0.68 and the (cell, heading) x {left,right,step} state space is handed over by the statement; no re-modelling insight is involved

drop.label: connected-components
drop.why: confidence 0.6; the open component is the arena the robot explores, not a technique applied, and a searcher for connected-components problems would not want a WF interactive localisation problem

add.label: simulation
add.why: the decision mechanism is carrying every consistent (cell, heading) candidate through the same actions and filtering by each observation; 'yes' fires exactly when all survivors share a cell. That belief-state tracking is essential and the vocabulary has no closer word for it

reviews.review_rationale: Re-derived: all survivors report the same d, so a relative-frame plan is legal for all (step iff d>0), actions are injective so only observations split the set, and once the survivors share one relative component shape they are bisimilar forever, so the only remaining lever is walking to a common fixed point of the surviving rotations (finite components admit no translational automorphism), else 'no'. The proposer's Moore-machine minimisation check on 250 maps and every-start-state run on 155 maps passed on my rerun, all three samples reproduce, and the round budget is safe: at most 3 scan turns plus two traversals of at most 3 rounds per cell gives <=8 per cell, ~80k worst case against 100k, with 60202 measured on the fully open 100x100.

Systematic: the proposers attach 'confidence 0.55-0.75' scaffolding labels (modular-arithmetic, parity-argument, graph-modeling, connected-components, greedy) that name the problem's surroundings rather than its technique; I dropped every one of those and kept only labels a searcher for that term would be glad to find.
